query: For a high-entropy alloy designed as a single-phase solid solution and exhibiting a favorable strength–ductility combination, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to preserve toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading? Explain the hypothesized mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the same alloy tested under identical conditions without the intervention, define the applicable exposure and loading regime, identify supporting evidence from prior observations, and specify an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of carbon to a high-entropy alloy will preserve toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading by promoting a twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) effect.
generation.conditions: Thermal exposure at 800 °C for up to 10 weeks and subsequent loading
generation.mechanism: The TWIP effect hinders dislocation slip, delays necking, and enhances work hardening, leading to improved toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved toughness compared to the same alloy without carbon addition
generation.boundary: Thermal exposure at 800 °C for up to 10 weeks and subsequent loading
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of the TWIP effect and its interaction with thermal exposure and loading is not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the toughness of high-entropy alloys with and without carbon addition after thermal exposure and subsequent loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the toughness of the alloy with carbon addition is not improved compared to the alloy without carbon addition, the hypothesis is falsified

Question: How do simultaneous microalloying with carbon (C) and molybdenum (Mo) affect the microstructure evolution, phase stability, and mechanical properties of Co-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloys?. System: [Co40Cr25(FeNi)35−yMoy]100−xCx (x = 0, 0.5; y = 3, 4, 5 at.%) HEAs. Processing: Vacuum arc melting of pure elements (≥99.9 wt.%) under Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, melted five times for homogeneity, solution treated at 1200 °C for 2 h, water quenched, and hot rolled with 70% reduction. Test conditions: Room temperature uniaxial tensile testing at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; XRD (20° to 100°, 40 kV, 40 mA); SEM and EBSD analysis. Findings: Without carbon, alloys exhibited an FCC + HCP dual-phase structure, whereas adding 0.5 at.% C resulted in a single FCC phase.; In non-carbon alloys, grain size increased from 17 μm to 47 μm as Mo content rose from 3 to 5 at.%.; The Mo4C0.5 alloy showed a significant decrease in grain size compared to other compositions after carbon addition.; In the Mo5C0.5 alloy, Mo content exceeded the solid solution limit, leading to the formation of Mo carbides.; The Mo4C0.5 alloy achieved a yield strength of 757 MPa, tensile strength of 1186
